kernels.definition: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

definitionAnchor.quote: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price

facts.text: Demand is elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one.

anchor.quote: Demand is described as elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one

facts.text: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes.

anchor.quote: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes

facts.text: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity.

anchor.quote: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity

kernels.definition: A demand curve shows the quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding other factors constant.

definitionAnchor.quote: the quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to purchase at each price, holding all other factors constant

facts.text: Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand.

anchor.quote: Demand curves typically slope downward, reflecting the law of demand

facts.text: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, while a change in income or tastes shifts the curve.

anchor.quote: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve

kernels.definition: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers.

definitionAnchor.quote: the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers

facts.text: At the equilibrium price the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and the price has no tendency to change.

anchor.quote: the opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced and there is no tendency for the price to change

facts.text: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus that pushes it down; a price below creates a shortage that pushes it up.

anchor.quote: a surplus pushes it down, and when the price is below equilibrium a shortage pushes it up

kernels.definition: A wage-price spiral is a self-reinforcing cycle in which rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further.

definitionAnchor.quote: rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and the higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further

facts.text: The wage-price spiral is positive feedback: an initial change is amplified rather than damped.

anchor.quote: positive feedback, in which an initial change is amplified rather than damped

facts.text: Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback drives the system further from where it started.

anchor.quote: positive feedback drives the system further from where it started

kernels.definition: Consumer choice theory models how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint.

definitionAnchor.quote: how a consumer maximizes utility subject to a budget constraint

facts.text: The consumer selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction.

anchor.quote: selects the affordable bundle of goods that yields the highest satisfaction

facts.text: At the optimal choice, utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so the consumer faces a tradeoff between goods.

anchor.quote: utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget, so the consumer faces a tradeoff between goods

kernels.definition: An economic model is a simplified representation of reality that keeps the features relevant to a question and discards the rest.

mcItems.q: When a product has many close substitutes, how does this affect its price elasticity of demand?
op: Demand becomes inelastic because consumers have many options
Demand becomes elastic because substitutes are plentiful
Demand remains unchanged regardless of substitute availability
Demand becomes inelastic because substitutes are few
mcItems.ex: The availability of close substitutes is a primary determinant of elasticity. This means demand is elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one.

op: Consumers have many alternatives to purchase the same item
Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes
The price change has no effect on the quantity demanded
Elasticity is determined solely by the percentage change in price
mcItems.ex: Necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers have few substitutes. This is because consumers have few substitutes.

mcItems.q: When a consumer alters their income, what happens to the demand curve?
op: The demand curve shifts because income affects purchasing power.
The demand curve moves along because income changes quantity demanded.
The demand curve shifts because income changes tastes.
The demand curve moves along because income changes the price.
mcItems.ex: A change in income causes a shift in the demand curve. A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve.

op: The demand curve shifts due to the price change.
The demand curve moves along reflecting the law of demand.
The demand curve shifts because the price change alters tastes.
The demand curve moves along because the price change alters income.
mcItems.ex: A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve. A change in income or tastes shifts the curve.

keyTerms.df: The law of demand describes the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity consumers desire to buy, typically showing an inverse relationship.

keyTerms.cx: The law of demand means that as the price of a good increases, the quantity demanded decreases.

mcItems.q: When a price is set above market equilibrium, what happens to the quantity demanded and supplied?
op: Quantity demanded increases while quantity supplied decreases
Quantity demanded decreases while quantity supplied increases
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at this price
Quantity demanded decreases while quantity supplied remains unchanged
mcItems.ex: A price above equilibrium generates a surplus that pushes the price down. This occurs because the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.

mcItems.q: If the price falls below the market equilibrium, what is the resulting pressure on the market?
op: The surplus shrinks and the price moves toward the upper limit
The shortage increases and the price moves toward the upper limit
The price remains stable because demand and supply are balanced
The quantity supplied increases while the quantity demanded decreases
mcItems.ex: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage that pushes the price up. This happens because the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied.

mcItems.q: When using a supply and demand model, what is the primary characteristic of the model's assumptions?
op: Assumptions are always perfectly accurate for the specific scenario.
Assumptions are simplified representations that may not hold exactly.
Assumptions are irrelevant if the question focuses on equilibrium.
Assumptions are only necessary when dealing with perfect competition.
mcItems.ex: Models such as supply and demand make assumptions, like rational choice or perfect competition, that do not hold exactly. A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand.

mcItems.q: Under what condition is an economic model considered misleading?

When a key assumption breaks during the analysis.
When the model simplifies reality to its core features.
When the model perfectly represents the underlying economic reality.
mcItems.ex: A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand. A model is misleading when a key assumption breaks.

mcItems.q: What condition describes demand being elastic?
op: The absolute value of elasticity is less than one
The absolute value of elasticity is greater than one
The price change is greater than the quantity change
Demand is perfectly inelastic regardless of price change
mcItems.ex: Demand is elastic when the absolute value of the elasticity is greater than one. This means quantity demanded changes significantly in response to price changes.

mcItems.q: What causes a movement along a demand curve?
op: A change in the good's price
B change in consumer income
C change in consumer tastes
D change in other factors
mcItems.ex: A change in the good's price causes a movement along the demand curve. A change in income or tastes shifts the curve instead.

mcItems.q: What causes a shift in a demand curve?
op: A change in the good's price
B a change in consumer income
C a change in tastes
D a change in quantity demanded
mcItems.ex: A change in tastes causes a shift in the demand curve. A change in price causes a movement along the existing demand curve.

mcItems.q: When a price is set above market equilibrium, what happens to the quantity demanded and supplied?
op: Quantity demanded increases while quantity supplied decreases
Quantity demanded decreases while quantity supplied increases
Quantity demanded equals quantity supplied at this price
Quantity demanded decreases while quantity supplied remains unchanged
mcItems.ex: A price above equilibrium generates a surplus that pushes the price down. This occurs because the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded.

mcItems.q: If the price falls below the market equilibrium, what is the resulting pressure on the market?
op: The surplus shrinks and the price moves toward the upper limit
The shortage increases and the price moves toward the upper limit
The price remains stable because demand and supply are balanced
The quantity supplied increases while the quantity demanded decreases
mcItems.ex: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage that pushes the price up. This happens because the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied.

keyTerms.df: The point where the quantity demanded by buyers exactly matches the quantity supplied by sellers.
keyTerms.eg: The market equilibrium occurs at the price where the quantity demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers.
keyTerms.mi: Market equilibrium is achieved when the price is set at the highest possible level for the good.
keyTerms.cx: Market equilibrium is achieved when the price is set where opposing pressures of demand and supply are balanced.

mcItems.q: What characterizes a wage-price spiral?
op: A self-reinforcing cycle where rising prices cause workers to demand higher wages
B a process where initial price increases lead to lower labor costs
C a system exhibiting negative feedback that stabilizes price levels
D a situation where wage demands decrease as inflation rises
mcItems.ex: A self-reinforcing cycle where rising prices cause workers to demand higher wages. This is positive feedback, not a stabilizing mechanism.

mcItems.q: How does the wage-price spiral operate?
op: A It functions as positive feedback, amplifying an initial change
B It acts as negative feedback, damping the initial price movement
C It is a simple linear relationship between wages and prices
D It results in equilibrium when both wages and prices are constant
mcItems.ex: It functions as positive feedback, amplifying an initial change. This means the system moves further from its starting point.

keyTerms.df: A self-reinforcing cycle where rising prices lead workers to demand higher wages, and higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further.
keyTerms.eg: Workers demand higher wages because prices rise, which causes firms to raise prices even further.
keyTerms.mi: A wage-price spiral is a system where rising prices cause workers to demand lower wages, and lower wages cause prices to fall.
keyTerms.cx: The wage-price spiral is a system where rising prices cause workers to demand higher wages, and higher wage costs lead firms to raise prices further.

keyTerms.df: An initial change is amplified rather than damped, driving the system further from where it started.
keyTerms.eg: An initial price increase causes a wage increase, which in turn causes even greater price increases.
keyTerms.mi: Positive feedback causes a system to stabilize quickly around a fixed equilibrium point.
keyTerms.cx: Positive feedback amplifies an initial change rather than damping it.

mcItems.q: When a consumer makes an optimal selection, what is the fundamental relationship between utility and the budget?
op: Utility increases indefinitely as the consumer spends more money
Utility is maximized when the budget constraint is not binding
Utility cannot increase without exceeding the budget
Utility is maximized by selecting the most expensive bundle
mcItems.ex: The consumer faces a tradeoff between goods at the optimal choice. This means utility cannot be increased without exceeding the budget.

mcItems.q: When using a supply and demand model, what is the primary characteristic of the model's assumptions?
op: Assumptions are always perfectly accurate for the specific scenario.
Assumptions are simplified representations that may not hold exactly.
Assumptions are irrelevant if the question focuses on equilibrium.
Assumptions are only necessary when dealing with perfect competition.
mcItems.ex: Models such as supply and demand make assumptions, like rational choice or perfect competition, that do not hold exactly. A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand.

mcItems.q: Under what condition is an economic model considered misleading?
op: When the model accurately predicts the observed outcome.
When a key assumption breaks during the analysis.
When the model simplifies reality to its core features.
When the model perfectly represents the underlying economic reality.
mcItems.ex: A model is useful when its assumptions are close enough for the question at hand. A model is misleading when a key assumption breaks.
